drafts.title: Why this history, and why we tell it from the shop
drafts.educational_claim: Handmade furniture did not jump from a workbench to a website. It moved through a sequence of selling rooms, and each room taught the buyer a different lie or a different truth.

drafts.title: Who is talking, and what a shop like this actually is
drafts.educational_claim: A custom furniture shop that sells through trade showrooms is not a store, not a factory in the Wayfair sense, and not a gallery. The speaker's job is to keep those categories from collapsing.

drafts.title: Four doors a handmade piece walked through
drafts.educational_claim: Consignment, wholesale, to-the-trade, and dropship are four different assignments of risk, title, and customer relationship. Mixing them is how shops go broke and buyers get confused.

drafts.title: Handmade, custom, wholesale, artisan — words that got stolen
drafts.educational_claim: Retail language drifted on purpose. Handmade, custom, wholesale, and artisan used to describe labor and contracts. After the platforms, they often describe a feeling.

drafts.title: America House — the first serious door for American craft
drafts.educational_claim: Before websites, American craft built a cooperative city shop so rural makers could reach metropolitan buyers. America House (1940–1971) is the ancestor of the gallery door.

drafts.title: Rhinebeck, Baltimore, and the ACC fair as a portable gallery
drafts.educational_claim: The American Craft Council fairs turned handmade retail into a temporary city with a jury, a booth fee, and two kinds of buyer: the public with a checkbook and the store with a wholesale order.

drafts.title: The gallery ticket — consignment, the wall, and the 50 percent myth
drafts.educational_claim: A craft gallery sells access to a taught buyer. Consignment keeps title with the maker; the split pays for rent, editing, and talk. The famous 50 percent is a habit, not a law.

drafts.title: When a table became art — studio furniture and the museum shadow
drafts.educational_claim: Mid-century studio furniture taught America that a chair could be a life's work. The art market that followed raised prices and also made ordinary usefulness look like a lesser category.

drafts.title: Why a dining table is a rude guest in a gallery
drafts.educational_claim: Scale, freight, sit-testing, and the time a table occupies a floor make dining furniture a poor fit for rooms designed around portable craft. That mismatch pushed serious tables toward showrooms and commissions.

drafts.title: The year you do not get in — juries, booths, and useful nos
drafts.educational_claim: Juries and booth fees are rationing systems. A no can be information about fit, fashion, or capacity. The internet's yes is not automatically kinder.

drafts.title: What a gallery taught a buyer that a website still cannot
drafts.educational_claim: Galleries taught looking, comparison, patience, and the right to ask who made the last two inches. Websites taught speed and a return policy. Those are not interchangeable educations.

drafts.title: The handoff — when furniture outgrew the gallery and needed a trade
drafts.educational_claim: As interior design professionalized, large handmade furniture moved from consignment walls to trade showrooms because designers needed repeatable catalog, net pricing, and a sample they could bring a client to.

drafts.title: To the trade — a badge is not a velvet rope for fun
drafts.educational_claim: To-the-trade means the professional is the customer. The restriction is usually on buying, not browsing. The system exists to split labor between maker, showroom, and designer.

drafts.title: The D&D and the design center — a mall that is not a mall
drafts.educational_claim: A design center is a cluster of wholesale showrooms for professionals. It is not High Point, not a department store, and not a craft fair. The D&D Building (1965) is the type specimen.

drafts.title: How a line gets into a showroom — and why most should not
drafts.educational_claim: Representation is a capacity deal. The showroom needs a line that will not embarrass them; the shop needs a room it can feed. Wanting every city is how lead times die.

drafts.title: Territory and exclusivity — the quiet fight over a name
drafts.educational_claim: Showroom exclusivity is a tool for protecting sales effort. It can also become a fence that keeps a maker from eating. The map is a contract, not a compliment.

drafts.title: List, net, and the multiplier — who is being paid for what
drafts.educational_claim: List is a published number. Net is the professional price. The gap is not automatically greed; it is a bundle of showroom labor, designer labor, and sometimes a fiction. Learn to parse the bundle.

drafts.title: The sample floor — pieces we build so other pieces can be believed
drafts.educational_claim: A showroom sample is a working argument, not inventory. It costs a shop real bench time, and it is how custom work stays honest across a continent.

drafts.title: Sidemarks, memos, acknowledgements — the paper that keeps a table honest
drafts.educational_claim: Trade paperwork exists because a commission has too many people to remember in their heads. Sidemarks, finish samples, and acknowledgements are how a shop refuses to guess.

drafts.title: Cold calls on Capitol Hill — how a shop finds a designer before it finds a building
drafts.educational_claim: Before a showroom list, a custom shop finds work by talking to designers one at a time. The call is a door. Most calls fail. The ones that do not become a practice.

drafts.title: Why we own the trucks — delivery as the last inch of making
drafts.educational_claim: Freight is where handmade furniture is most often ruined. A shop that delivers its own work is refusing to outsource the last inch of the object.

drafts.title: High Point — the twice-a-year city that is not a store
drafts.educational_claim: High Point Market, begun as the Southern Furniture Market in 1909, is a trade gathering. It is where wholesale relationships are made, not where the public shops a mall.

drafts.title: A market order is not a cart
drafts.educational_claim: A traditional market order moved title, terms, and a season's bet. A website cart moves a payment and a hope. Handmade shops that treated carts like market orders absorbed risk they did not price.

drafts.title: Tear sheets and catalogs — the photograph before the photograph
drafts.educational_claim: Trade catalogs and tear sheets taught the industry to sell from paper long before e-commerce. The web did not invent the picture. It deleted the person holding the picture.

drafts.title: eBay, Yahoo, and the first digital storefronts
drafts.educational_claim: Before Etsy and Wayfair, makers used eBay, Yahoo stores, and early personal sites as doors. Those doors taught payments and photographs. They did not solve furniture.

drafts.title: Photography became the showroom
drafts.educational_claim: Once the picture could take money, shops started building for the camera. That changed which objects got made, which defects were allowed, and who learned to look.

drafts.title: Freight is not shipping
drafts.educational_claim: Parcel shipping and furniture freight are different industries. Early e-commerce hid that difference behind a checkout line, and handmade tables paid for the confusion.

drafts.title: 2005 — a marketplace that actually meant handmade
drafts.educational_claim: Etsy launched in June 2005 as a Brooklyn-built marketplace for handmade goods. Its first gift to makers was a room that believed the word. Its first problem was scale.

drafts.title: Why a dining table never fit Etsy's jewelry economics
drafts.educational_claim: Etsy's fee structure, shipping culture, and browsing habit were built around portable, repeatable, parcel-scale objects. Furniture breaks each of those assumptions.

drafts.title: 2013 — the handmade wars
drafts.educational_claim: In October 2013 Etsy allowed sellers to hire and to apply to use manufacturers if they remained the design author. The fight was about whether handmade is labor or authorship.

drafts.title: Handmade, vintage, supplies — three buckets, one storefront
drafts.educational_claim: Etsy's public contract was three allowed kinds of goods. Furniture could be honest in all three and still confuse a buyer who thought the storefront meant one thing.

drafts.title: When the booth fee became an auction
drafts.educational_claim: A listing fee is rent. Promoted listings are an auction for oxygen. After ads, "organic" handmade discovery is a phrase, not a system.

drafts.title: Etsy Wholesale — the dream of a clean big-box door
drafts.educational_claim: Etsy Wholesale tried to connect growing sellers to retailers. It is the bridge sentence between craft-marketplace culture and the older wholesale pipe. Treat it as a chapter, not a current promise.

drafts.title: Overstock — from closeouts to fulfillment partners
drafts.educational_claim: Overstock began as an online closeout shop (D2, 1997; Overstock.com, 1999) and grew a fulfillment-partner model that let other people's inventory sit on their site. That is an early industrial dropship.

drafts.title: CSN Stores — two hundred websites, then one word
drafts.educational_claim: Wayfair began in 2002 as CSN Stores, a forest of niche sites, then consolidated into Wayfair.com in 2011. The catalog was a supplier network, not a warehouse of their own objects.

drafts.title: Dropship, said as a job description
drafts.educational_claim: Dropship assigns the customer to the website and the object to the shop. It is a job change, not a marketing channel. Shops that priced it like wholesale underpriced the job.

drafts.title: High Point as a recruiting office for catalogs
drafts.educational_claim: Platforms filled millions of SKUs by walking the old wholesale market and turning supplier catalogs into listings. The market's original buyer was a store. The new buyer was a website.

drafts.title: The SKU flood and the death of the edited floor
drafts.educational_claim: An edited floor teaches by exclusion. A seven-million-SKU catalog teaches by ranking. Handmade furniture got harder to see when exclusion left the building.

drafts.title: MAP, private label, and whose name is on the box
drafts.educational_claim: Minimum advertised price and private label decide whether a shop's work can be recognized. Platforms often wanted the object without the name. Showrooms wanted the name without a public discount war.

drafts.title: Returns, chargebacks, and a table that already left the shop
drafts.educational_claim: Furniture returns are a second making. Chargebacks are a third party rewriting the acknowledgement. Platform policies built for parcels treat both as normal.

drafts.title: Walking away from the pipe
drafts.educational_claim: Leaving a platform pipe is a capacity decision. It costs orders. It buys back the customer, the name, and the right to say no. Not every shop can afford the walk. Every shop should price it.

drafts.title: Four prices for the same table
drafts.educational_claim: The same object can carry four honest prices depending on door, livings, risk, and teaching. A cheaper picture is often a different bundle, not a bargain on the same bundle.

drafts.title: What American made meant in 1999, and what a caption means now
drafts.educational_claim: American made used to imply a building, a payroll, and a dock. After global supply chains and caption culture, the phrase can mean a brand office, a final assembly, or a hope. Ask for the building.

drafts.title: Keep the house standing — what this channel is for
drafts.educational_claim: The history is a tool. Use it to read a door, keep a shop alive while it changes, and refuse stolen words. The channel teaches the route, then shows the work.
